01

What Obertura is

Obertura (Catalan/Spanish for “opening”) is a focused chess-opening trainer — a slimmed-down, openings-only take on apps like Lotus/Chessable. It is a personal project built phone-first, and it does one thing well: it helps you build a repertoire that is genuinely yours, drill it, and remember it.

Build

Create your own opening lines by hand on a real board, or seed them from a bundled library, from your own imported games, from the engine, or from scouting an opponent.

Train

Play a line once to confirm it, then drill it. A spaced-repetition scheduler (SM-2) brings your weakest moves back exactly when you’re about to forget them — never random.

See it whole

Every line is a tree of moves with branches and variations. Openings are recognised and named automatically from a bundled database — no internet needed.

Measure it

Streaks, win-rate by opening, remembered-moves-over-time, puzzle rating and “needs attention” lists turn practice into visible progress.

The guiding constraintsEverything runs in the browser. There is no server and no account — your repertoire lives in the phone’s own storage. It installs to the home screen like a native app. It’s free to run and built as a slow-burn side project, so scope is guarded carefully.

02

The visual design system

Obertura has a deliberate, warm visual identity: think a well-thumbed opening book on a wooden table. Everything below is generated from the app’s actual CSS variables (“design tokens”), so it is the real system, not a mock-up. Flip the theme switch at the top to see it adapt.

2.1 Design philosophy

Paper, not plastic

The page background carries a faint paper speckle texture, surfaces are warm creams and parchments rather than pure white, and the mood is analog and studious — never a cold “tech” grey.

The board is sacred

The chessboard squares are never themed. They stay the same warm wood in light, dark, and every other theme, so the thing you actually stare at is always familiar. Only the surrounding “chrome” changes.

Phone-first & thumb-friendly

Every tappable control is at least 44 px tall. Layouts are single-column, the primary navigation sits at the bottom where thumbs reach, and panels are swipeable.

One system, applied everywhere

A single spacing scale, one card, one button family, one filter bar — reused across screens rather than reinvented. This keeps the app feeling coherent and the code small.

One source of truthEvery colour in the app resolves to a CSS variable. JavaScript picks the theme and writes data-theme="light|dark|game|gamer" onto the page; the CSS only ever reads that attribute. That’s why the switch above can re-skin this entire document instantly.

Three building blocks compose almost every screen. The section — a soft wrapper with a hairline border, a very faint fill and a small title row — is what kills the “stacked boxes” feeling. The card is the one surface for a piece of content. The row is the standard list item.

2.11 Chess-specific components

Move strip (notation)

A horizontally-scrolling PGN-style strip. The active move is highlighted amber; branches render as parenthesised variations; annotation marks (!, ?!, ??…) and a note dot appear inline.

Every saved line shows a mini-board of its final position and a five-pip confidence meter (how well spaced-repetition thinks you know it).

Used throughout Explore, scouting and the builder’s “My games”/“Library” tabs: a sage/grey/brick bar shows how a move actually scores (from your games or from master statistics).

03

App shell & navigation

Everything lives inside one screen. There are no page reloads — tapping a tab just swaps which “view” is visible. The shell is three fixed pieces: a header on top, the active view in the middle, and a tab bar at the bottom.

3.1 Header

  • Back arrow (left) — appears only when you’ve drilled into something (a line, an opponent dossier). Honours the phone’s hardware/gesture back button too.
  • Title — the wordmark on the main screens, or the current context (line name, opponent) when deeper in.
  • Settings (person icon, right) — opens the Settings screen.
  • Save line — a green button that appears in the header only inside the Builder, so saving is always one reach away.

3.2 Bottom tab bar — the five destinations

The primary navigation. The active tab is amber. These five are the top-level map of the whole app.

TabIconWhat it is
Train⚡ lightningThe home screen. Where you actually practise.
My Lines♟ pawnYour saved repertoire — every line you’ve built.
Explore🧭 compassFind new material: recommendations, packs, traps, scouting, the library, engine sparring.
My games▦ gridYour imported real games, and the analyser hand-off.
Statistics📊 barsProgress: streaks, win-rate, ratings, what needs attention.
NoteThe Builder / Analyser (section 4.3) has no tab of its own — it’s the workspace you land in from “build a line”, opening a saved line, or analysing a game. It is arguably the single most important screen in the app.

3.3 The FAB & transient UI

Floating action button (＋)

A green ＋ pinned bottom-right on the main lists. Tapping it fans out quick “create / import” actions over a dimmed backdrop. It hides itself during celebrations and drills so it never sits over the action.

Boot splash

On launch, the app icon pulses on the themed background until the first screen’s data is ready — so you never see a bare “Loading…”.

Toasts

Small, self-dismissing messages at the bottom (“Analysis complete”, “Live analysis off”) for feedback that doesn’t need a dialog.

Sheets & dialogs

Editing (name, tags, notes) happens in bottom sheets that lift above the on-screen keyboard. Destructive actions use a confirm dialog.

04

The screens — front-end UX

This is the heart of the guide: every screen, what it shows, and every feature on it. Reference any sub-heading number to point precisely at what you want changed.

4.1 Train

The default screen and the app’s centre of gravity. At the very top sits a 2×2 grid of game modes, each with its own accent colour when active. Tapping one swaps the pane below it:

  • Openings (accent amber) — drilling your repertoire lines. The default.
  • Puzzles (bronze) — rated tactics from Lichess.
  • Mistake retry (ember) — the exact positions your real games went wrong.
  • End game (its own accent) — endgame puzzles + classic endgames vs the engine.

4.1.1  Openings pane

  • Daily challenge card — a small set of daily tasks (3 lines to remember, 5 rated puzzles, plus mistakes-to-fix when you have any), with your day-streak alongside. Collapses to “done — keep training ✓” when finished, and each task chains “Next task →”.
  • “Due now” hero — a two-stat panel (Due now · Reviewed today) with a big Start review button. It hides entirely when nothing is due, so the screen is honest about whether there’s work.
  • Practise modes — cards for Fix mistakes (single missed moves, with a due-count), Time attack (beat your best in 1 / 3 / 5 minutes, personal bests shown), Fresh lines (full runs of your newest lines) and Weak spots (your weakest lines).
  • Forgotten-moves carousel — a swipeable board per time window (Today / This week / All time) showing the move you miss most, with an arrow on the move and a Fix it repeat-drill.
  • Training list — every line in training, with the shared filter bar (colour · sort · group-by-opening). “In training” collapses behind its header; grouped views can pause a whole opening family at once.

4.1.2  The drill loop & success screens

Drilling walks a full line move by move: you play your side, the app replies. A wrong move gives brick-red feedback and the sage-green right answer; a soft sound can confirm right/wrong. Sessions are split into rounds so progress banks mid-session. Every mode ends on a playful, gamified success screen (confetti, count-ups) that lists the openings reviewed with correct/incorrect tallies.

4.1.3  Puzzles

Rated tactics powered by the Lichess puzzle database. Your own puzzle rating ladder, a “solved today” count, a daily easy→medium→hard ladder, and a Time attack (3 mistakes and you’re out; puzzles get harder as you go). After a puzzle, a discrete “Analyse position” opens it in the analyser.

4.1.4  Mistake retry

Training that reaches into your own games. A user-triggered scan (“Analyse my games”) walks each imported game — Lichess cloud first, local engine on misses — and finds four kinds of spot: opening blunders, punish the opening, missed wins, and game-losing blunders. The retry drill then re-serves those exact positions puzzle-style: your actual move as a red arrow, a two-stage hint, instant checking against the engine’s stored top-3, badge + confetti on a clean find. A carousel surfaces the latest unfixed spot per category.

4.1.5  End game

Two pillars that need no imported games: Endgame puzzles (rated Lichess puzzles filtered by theme — Rook / Pawn / Queen / Minor — on their own separate rating ladder) and Classic endgames (a bundled list of the fundamentals you load and play out against the engine, with the Lichess 7-piece tablebase as the ground-truth judge). Progress is ticked per position.

4.2 My Lines

Your whole repertoire. A top toggle switches between Saved lines and From my games (suggestions lifted from what you actually play). Below that, the shared filter bar: colour (All / White / Black), a sort menu, and a group-by-opening control that cycles flat → by family → compact.

Each line is a card with: its name, a mini-board of the final position, its opening name, tags, a confidence meter, when it was last trained, and a Training ON/OFF switch. A “Due” pill flags lines the scheduler wants back. A pencil edits; a trash deletes (with confirm). Tapping the card (or the eye) opens it in the Builder to step through.

4.3 The Builder / Analyser

The workspace where lines are made and games are studied. Layout, top to bottom:

  • The board — a fixed square you make moves on. Legal-move dots, last-move highlight, promotion picker, flip.
  • A draggable sheet — a Google-Maps-style panel that sits under the board and pulls up over it for more room.
  • A swipeable carousel of tabs inside the sheet (below).
  • A bottom control dock — flip board, Analyse (game review), engine-everywhere toggle, watch/play the line, and step ◀ ▶ arrows.

The carousel tabs

Line

The line itself: title (with live opening name), the move strip, tags, a per-move note, the game-review analysis block, and the training toggle + delete.

Engine

Stockfish evaluation: a winning-chances bar, the top candidate moves, and up to three candidate arrows on the board (default off, behind a toggle).

Library

A board explorer over the bundled opening book plus deeper online continuations — the popular replies from this position, with real master games.

My games

How you have actually continued from this exact position in your imported games, each reply with a win-rate WDL bar and a game count.

Scouting

A board browser through a scouted opponent’s real moves from here (hidden entirely when scouting is off).

Editing & annotating

  • Title & tags — a pencil renames the line; a tag icon opens a sheet with suggested chips plus every tag you’ve used before.
  • Notes & marks — a per-move note sheet holds a written reminder and one of the six standard annotation symbols (!!, !, !?, ?!, ?, ??).
  • Game Review — a live toggle that grades every move on the board (and each new one as you play it), writing the coloured badges from 2.12. Auto-stores onto the game record.
  • Save — the green header button. The builder saves exactly one line; a divergent edit truncates the branch so what you save is what you see.
  • Watch line — plays the line back to you automatically.

4.4 Explore

Where new material comes from. Three pillars, tabbed like My Lines:

Recommended

Openings you play a lot but score poorly in, built from your imported games — “build a solid line here and train it”.

Packs & Traps

The curated library: starter packs and a relevance-ranked library of famous opening traps, both filterable by colour and tag.

Scouting

Scout up to ten opponents from their public games. Each opens a full-screen dossier: their most-played openings per colour, W-D-L bars, a scouting report (their weak/strong openings + what to play), and auto-built opening maps with per-move stats and a “Go deeper” control. A Prepare flow produces opponent-tagged reply lines.

Explore also hosts the Opening library browser and Build with the engine (spar against Stockfish — Surprise me / From my games / Pure engine opening modes, with a Solid · Aggressive · Random suggest control) → open the result straight into the builder.

4.5 My games

Your imported real games from Chess.com and Lichess. A full-screen import loader (with your profile picture and a review graph) pulls games with date/colour ranges and a scan step before committing. Game cards match the My Lines size, carry a thin won/loss border and a numeric date, and can be tagged and grouped. Tapping one opens it in the analyser; a finished analysis is stored on the game so reopening is instant. You can also add a game manually or paste a PGN.

4.6 Statistics

Progress, kept honestly. Top to bottom:

  • Streak card — day-streak with a weekday activity strip and an expandable “training activity” heatmap.
  • Stat tiles — Lines · Training · Mastered.
  • Openings — “Remembered moves over time” (a graph, with a marker on days you added lines so a dip reads as fresh material, not forgetting) and a most-forgotten-move board.
  • Puzzles — puzzle rating over time (Week / Month / All carousel), solved, accuracy, and a “best run” box.
  • Win rate by opening — your real results per opening with sage/amber/brick bars and game counts, plus accuracy-by-opening.
  • Needs attention — the specific lines the scheduler thinks are slipping, with a one-tap Drill.

4.8 Onboarding (first run)

A brand-new user with no lines doesn’t see an empty Train screen. Instead a first-launch flow seeds a repertoire: a short intro walkthrough, then starter packs and game-based line suggestions (gated at six lines / six packs, packs collapsed by default, each with a mini-board). Pedagogical empty states across the four main screens explain what each does and route you to the fix. Once six lines are in training, the normal hub takes over for good.

05

The technical stack — explained plainly

This section is for you, Marçal — no code knowledge assumed. The goal is that you understand what each piece does and why it’s there, so a conversation about changing something technical isn’t a black box.

5.1 The big picture

Obertura is a web app that behaves like a native app. Everything runs inside the phone’s browser. There is deliberately no server — nothing to pay for, nothing to maintain, and your data never leaves your device unless you explicitly back it up. The pieces stack like this:

Interface What you see & touch

The board, the screens, the buttons — drawn with chessground and styled by the design system in section 2.

Logic The app’s brain

Written in TypeScript. Enforces the rules of chess (chess.js), runs the spaced-repetition scheduler, and orchestrates every screen.

Storage Your repertoire

Saved in IndexedDB, a database built into the phone’s browser. On the device, private, and works offline.

Occasional internet Optional helpers

The Stockfish engine (in the browser), and calls to Lichess / Chess.com for opening data, puzzles, evaluations and importing games. Optional Google Drive backup.

What is a PWA?A Progressive Web App is a website that can be “installed” to your home screen and launched full-screen like any other app — no App Store needed. Obertura ships a manifest (its name, icons, colours) so Android offers “Add to Home screen”. It runs online-only for now; true offline support is a deliberate “later”.

5.2 Build tool & language

Vite

The build tool. During development it serves the app with instant refresh; for release it bundles everything into a small, optimised set of files. Think of it as the workshop that turns the source into the finished, fast-loading app.

TypeScript (vanilla)

The language the app is written in — JavaScript with a safety net that catches mistakes before they ship. Deliberately no big framework (React/Vue) for v1: plain code keeps the app small and fast, which matters on a phone.

5.3 The chess libraries

chessground

Lichess’s open-source board component. It draws the board and pieces, handles dragging, legal-move dots, arrows, and animations. It’s the same board engine Lichess itself uses — battle-tested and beautiful.

chess.js

The rules referee. It knows what moves are legal, detects check/mate, understands promotion and castling, and reads/writes standard notation (PGN/FEN). chessground draws; chess.js judges.

5.4 Storage on the device

IndexedDB is a small database built into every phone browser. Obertura uses it (through a thin wrapper) to store your lines, imported games, opponents, stats, streaks and ratings. Because it’s on the device: it’s private, it’s free, and it works with no signal. The trade-off — and the reason backups matter — is that clearing the browser’s data would erase it.

Why backups existSince there’s no server, your repertoire only lives in one place. That’s why Settings → Data offers a JSON export/import and an optional Google Drive backup (section 5.7).

5.5 The Stockfish engine

Stockfish is the world’s strongest open-source chess engine. Obertura runs a lightweight WebAssembly build of it inside your browser — nothing is sent anywhere. It runs in a Web Worker, a background thread, so the board never freezes while it thinks. It powers the eval bar, candidate arrows, move grading, the mistake scan, and playing out endgames. There are guards (time budgets, a cloud circuit-breaker) so it stays fast on a phone.

5.6 Outside data sources

SourceUsed for
Lichess opening explorerPopular continuations & real master games in the Library tab.
Lichess cloud evalFast position evaluations (falls back to on-device Stockfish).
Lichess puzzlesThe rated Puzzles & endgame-puzzle modes.
Lichess tablebaseThe ground-truth judge for Classic endgames (7-piece).
Chess.com & Lichess game APIsImporting your real games and scouting opponents.
Bundled opening databaseInstant, offline opening names (see 5.9) — no API call.

Connecting a Lichess account (optional OAuth) raises the cloud-eval rate limit. Obertura is not affiliated with Chess.com or Lichess — it simply reads their public data.

5.7 Cloud backup (Google Drive)

An optional way to keep your repertoire safe and move it between devices. Connecting via a Google sign-in popup lets the app write a single backup file into a hidden app-data folder — the app can never see your real Drive files. There’s “Back up now”, “Restore from Drive”, and an auto-backup toggle that quietly uploads ~30 s after any change. It stays inert until a (free) Google client ID is configured. Still no server anywhere — Drive is just the user’s own storage.

5.9 The data model

Understanding this makes every screen click into place. Your repertoire is a small nested structure:

// two repertoires: "my White lines" & "my Black lines"
Line {
  name, tags[], colour, openingName,
  confidence, lastTrained, inTraining,
  tree: // a Line is a TREE of moves, not a list
    MoveNode {
      san, uci, fen,
      children[], // branches / variations
      note?, annotation?,
      review: { ease, interval, reps, lapses, due }
    }
}
  • A line is a tree. Each move (MoveNode) can have several children — that’s how branches and sidelines are stored. The move strip renders the main line inline and branches in parentheses.
  • san / uci / fen — three ways to name a move & position: human notation, machine notation, and a full snapshot of the board. Having the fen on every node is what lets the app name openings and look up statistics instantly.
  • review — the spaced-repetition bookkeeping lives on each move node. A “due line” is any line containing a due move.

5.10 Spaced repetition (SM-2)

The scheduler is a classic SM-2 algorithm (the SuperMemo method behind Anki). In plain terms: each move you drill has an ease and an interval. Answer it well and the interval stretches — you’ll see it again in days, then weeks. Miss it and the interval collapses so it comes back soon. This is why training is never random: the app spends your time on exactly the moves you’re about to forget. Confidence pips and “needs attention” are just this bookkeeping made visible.

A quiet but important detail: the app ships a suite of self-tests (over a hundred) covering the scheduler, tree logic, importers, accuracy model and more — so refactors don’t silently break the maths. There’s a self-test panel in Settings → Diagnostics.

06

How to reference a section

This is the whole point of the document: a shared map so you can point at exactly what you want improved, and I know precisely where it lives in the app and the code.

Say it like this

  • “Rework 2.2 — I want a fifth theme.”
  • “The 4.1.4 mistake-retry hint is too subtle.”
  • “On 4.3, the carousel tabs are hard to reach one-handed.”
  • “4.6 Statistics — the win-rate bars need clearer labels.”
  • “Explain 5.7 Drive backup again before we build it.”

The number tells me

2.x → the design system (colours, components, type).
3.x → the shell & navigation.
4.x → a specific screen and its features.
5.x → something technical / under the hood.

Every heading on this page carries its number, and the contents list up top links straight to it.
